newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS-Merrill Lynch sees private wealth boom.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Merrill Lynch sees private wealth boom.

text.p: Merrill Lynch and Co Inc Bank, reporting a 56 percent growth in private assets managed in Switzerland last year, said on Tuesday that private banking was booming globally with Southeast Asia leading the world's new wealth creation.

Merrill Lynch Bank Suisse, based in Geneva, said total assets managed in Switzerland grew 51 percent in 1996 to 10.3 billion Swiss francs ($7 billion), including 4.0 billion Swiss francs ($2.7 billion) in private assets, up 56 percent over 1995.

The bank said private wealth managed in Switzerland was forecast to grow by between 20 and 25 percent in 1997. Growth was attributed in part to market performance. Growth in new clients was 20 percent in 1996.

Michael Giles, chairman of Merrill Lynch International Banks London, said in an interview in Zurich that he expected private assets managed globally by the bank, now at $50 billion, to grow by an average annual 20 percent in the next five years.
The bank estimates global growth rates in the industry at more than 10 percent a year, with emerging markets led by the Far East taking the lead in new private wealth creation.
"Southeast Asia is the fastest growing area for us in terms of private banking. Our business is growing in every one of these markets, particularly in China," Giles told Reuters.
"The emergence of China is creating entrepreneurial wealth not only in China but in the whole of Southeast Asia."

Giles did not give a breakdown for business in Asia. In Hong Kong, he said there had been some flight of private wealth out of the British colony ahead of China's takeover on July 1 but that this had been much less than anticipated.
Europe and Latin America had the biggest slice of Merrill Lynch's private banking business with 40 percent share each but emerging markets were set to take the lead soon, he said.
Middle East also remained a growth area while business was slowing down in the United States.
"Growth rates in private wealth creation will continue to be higher in emerging markets than in traditional European markets," Giles said.
"We're already growing in these markets and expect to continue to grow. We expect higher growth rates in the international private banking business for the foreseeable future than our U.S. business."
Private banking concentrates on "high net-worth individuals" -- people with liquid assets, or easily available cash, of at least $500,000.

Accountancy and consulting firm Price Waterhouse estimates the global market for these people at somewhere between $17 and $20 trillion. Of this, probably between $4 and $6 trillion is estimated to be in Europe.
The arrival of U.S. private banking giants has increased competition in the Swiss industry, put downward pressure on margins and hurt fee incomes, bankers say.
Giles said fee erosion was not an issue for Merrill Lynch in Switzerland.
"We are certainly not immune from competition, but I expect our growth rate in Switzerland at rates above the average of Swiss banks," he said.
